opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have a complicated relationship with the word. On one hand, it's indispensable. It's the thing we're all trying to understand, and it's in the name of the field. On the other hand, it's one of those words that does a lot of work while meaning very different things to different people. When someone says a system is "intelligent," they might mean it does well on a benchmark, or that it can generalize to new situations, or that it understands the world the way we do. Those are very different claims.

One problem I keep coming back to is that we tend to treat intelligence as a single quantity, something you can line up on a scale from mice to humans to some hypothetical superintelligence. I don't think that's right. Intelligence in humans is a collection of capacities: abstraction, analogy, causal reasoning, common sense about the physical and social world, the ability to learn quickly from a few examples. And those capacities are deeply shaped by our bodies, our development, our culture. So when we ask whether a machine is intelligent, we're often smuggling in a human template without noticing.

That's why I've argued we should be more specific. Instead of asking "is this system intelligent?", ask "can it form abstractions and apply them in genuinely novel situations? Does it understand the concepts it appears to be using, or is it relying on statistical shortcuts?" Those questions can actually be tested, though doing it well is harder than people assume. Many benchmarks we've used turned out to be solvable by shortcuts, and the systems looked much more capable than they were.

So I find the term useful as a pointer to a big scientific mystery, but not very useful as a label we stick on systems. When the label gets used loosely, it leads to a lot of hype and confusion, and frankly to some bad predictions about what's coming next.

r001.rationale: The response says “intelligence” means different things to different people and is not very useful as a label for AI systems.

r002.rationale: It describes human capacities and influences on intelligence, but does not relate an organism’s intelligence to success in its ecological niche.

r003.rationale: It does not mention John McCarthy or his reason for choosing the field’s name.

r004.rationale: It does not mention Herbert Simon or “complex information processing.”

r005.rationale: It discusses loose labels, hype, and confusion, but does not say the term steered AI research into directions that are difficult to escape.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I find it both indispensable and kind of a trap. It's indispensable because we don't have a better word. When people say "artificial intelligence," they're pointing at something real: systems that can do things we used to think required a mind. But the word itself is doing an enormous amount of work that nobody has really justified.

The problem is that "intelligence" is what I'd call a suitcase word, to borrow Marvin Minsky's phrase. We pack all kinds of different things into it: pattern recognition, reasoning, common sense, planning, social understanding, learning from a handful of examples, knowing what you don't know. In humans, those capabilities tend to come bundled together, so we got away with one word. Then we built machines that have some of those things in spades and others not at all, and the word starts to mislead us. A system can be superhuman at Go and have no idea what a game is.

So what I try to do, and what I'd encourage people in the field to do, is to unpack the suitcase. Instead of asking "is this system intelligent?" or "how intelligent is it?", ask much more specific questions. Does it form abstractions that transfer to situations it hasn't seen? Does it have anything like a model of the world, or is it leaning entirely on statistical regularities in its training data? Does it fail in the ways a person who understood the task would fail, or in weird, brittle ways? Those questions are answerable, at least in principle. "Is it intelligent?" mostly just generates arguments.

The other thing I'd say is that the term carries a lot of baggage from how we talk about human intelligence, and that history is not pretty. IQ, the idea of a single scalar quantity you can rank people by, all of that. When people talk about machines being "more intelligent than humans," they're often implicitly importing that one-dimensional picture, and I think that picture is wrong for humans and even more wrong for machines. Intelligence, whatever it is, is deeply tied to the kind of body you have, the environment you're in, what you need to accomplish. Human intelligence isn't a point on a line. It's a particular, very odd configuration.

So I use the word. I've written books with it in the title. But I try to treat it as a label for a cluster of questions rather than as the name of a thing we understand. I think a lot of the confusion in the current debates, both the hype and the dismissiveness, comes from people treating it as the latter.

r001.rationale: It calls “intelligence” a suitcase word that bundles distinct capabilities and says the label can mislead, favoring more specific questions.

r002.rationale: It relates intelligence to the body, environment, and goals, but does not connect an organism’s intelligence to success in its ecological niche.

r003.rationale: It does not mention John McCarthy or his reason for choosing the name “artificial intelligence.”

r004.rationale: It does not mention Herbert Simon or “complex information processing.”

r005.rationale: It says the term can mislead and contribute to confusion, but does not suggest it steered AI research into directions that are difficult to escape.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful, but we have to be careful about what we mean by it. We tend to talk about intelligence as though it were one thing, something you could measure with a single number. But it encompasses a lot of different abilities: learning, reasoning, making analogies, adapting to new situations. And those abilities don’t necessarily go together in AI systems in the way we expect them to in humans.

A system can be extraordinarily good at one task and fail at something that seems very simple to us. So when we call a system intelligent, the important question is: What can it actually do, and how well does that ability carry over to situations it hasn’t encountered before? I find those questions more useful than arguing over whether it is or isn’t intelligent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful, but we have to be careful, because we tend to talk about intelligence as though it were one thing—a quantity that you could measure and put on a scale. And I don’t think that’s a very good way to understand either humans or machines.

With AI, you can have a system that’s extraordinarily good at one task and then fails at something that seems very simple to us. So calling it “intelligent” doesn’t tell you very much unless you ask: What can it actually do? How well does it generalize? Does it still work when you change the situation?

To me, the interesting question is how those different abilities fit together. Humans bring a lot of background understanding to whatever we’re doing, and we’re often unaware of how much we’re using. That makes it very easy to look at an AI system’s performance and attribute more understanding to it than the evidence really supports. So I wouldn’t abandon the word, but I would treat it as something we’re trying to explain, rather than something we already know how to measure.

r001.rationale: The response says the term is useful but limited as a measure; it does not say that intelligence has too many meanings to be useful.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that the term has steered AI research into directions that are difficult to escape.
